title: Tipping at Restaurants
resolution: Resolved: Restaurants in the United States should replace tipping with service-included prices.
summary: In most American restaurants, a large part of a server's pay comes from tips. Some restaurants have tried raising menu prices and ending tips instead. Which way is better for workers and diners?

background.p: Under federal law, an employer may pay a tipped worker a cash wage as low as $2.13 an hour, as long as tips bring the worker up to the federal minimum wage of $7.25; if they don't, the employer must make up the difference. States set their own rules. As of July 2026, the U.S. Department of Labor lists seven states (Alaska, California, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, Oregon and Washington) that require the full state minimum wage before tips.

Cornell professor Michael Lynn, who has studied tipping for decades, found that tip percentages are only weakly related to how customers rate the service. In 2015, Union Square Hospitality Group, a well-known New York restaurant company, ended tipping and raised menu prices, partly so kitchen workers could share in the money. It brought tipping back in 2020, when the pandemic cut restaurant sales. Lynn's research found that some restaurants that dropped tipping saw their online service ratings fall, more so when they added a service charge than when they raised menu prices.

disputed.q: Would servers earn more or less without tips?
positions: At busy full-service restaurants, servers often earn more from tips than most restaurants could pay in wages, so many would earn less.

Supporters reply that tips swing from shift to shift and restaurant to restaurant, and that servers at slower restaurants, and kitchen workers who get few or no tips, could earn more and more steadily.

terms.def: The part of the minimum wage that an employer may count from tips instead of paying in cash wages. Under federal law, up to $5.12 an hour.
Menu prices that already include the cost of service, so no tip is expected. Sometimes called "hospitality included."
A set percentage added to the bill by the restaurant. Unlike a tip, it isn't voluntary and belongs to the restaurant, which decides how to pay it out.

terms.term: Front of house / back of house
terms.def: Restaurant workers who serve guests (servers, bartenders, hosts) and those who work out of sight (cooks, dishwashers).

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Service-included prices give workers steady pay, share it more fairly, and show diners the real price.

args.warrant: Tips rise and fall with the weather, the shift and the mood of each table. A wage built into prices lets workers plan rent and bills.
args.evidence: Studies of earnings volatility among tipped workers; the Economic Policy Institute's comparison of poverty rates for tipped workers in states with different tipped wages (2014).
args.response: The negative answers that steady pay can also be lower pay; many servers would trade higher average earnings for steadiness only if the total were the same.

args.warrant: If tips barely track how good the service was, they don't reward good work. They mostly reflect things the server doesn't control, like the size of the bill and the customer's habits.
args.evidence: Michael Lynn's research at Cornell finding tip percentages are only weakly related to customers' ratings of service.
args.response: The negative replies that even a weak link is some link, and servers still have a reason to be attentive, which a flat wage doesn't give.

args.warrant: Cooks and dishwashers help make every meal but usually share little of the tips. Building service into prices lets the restaurant pay the whole team.
args.evidence: Union Square Hospitality Group's stated reason for its 2015 policy: back-of-house workers couldn't share in guests' generosity.
args.response: The negative points out that the same company brought tipping back in 2020, and that tip pools already let restaurants share tips more widely in many states.

args.claim: Diners should see the real price.
args.warrant: A menu that lists $15 when the meal costs about $18 after the tip makes prices harder to compare. Most countries print the full price.
args.evidence: Consumer surveys on frustration with tipping requests; restaurant pricing practices in countries without tipping.
args.response: The negative replies that American diners are used to tipping and know to add it, and that higher menu prices can drive them to competitors who still list lower prices.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Tipping lets diners reward service, lets skilled servers earn well, and keeps menu prices low.

args.claim: Many servers earn more with tips.
args.warrant: At busy restaurants, tips can add up to more per hour than a restaurant could afford in wages. Ending tips would cut pay for the workers the policy aims to help.
args.evidence: Lynn's 2018 interview giving New York server earnings of about $25 to $30 an hour, well above cooks' pay; surveys of servers' views on tipping.
args.response: The affirmative answers that those figures describe busy city restaurants; across the country, tipped workers in states with low cash wages have higher poverty rates.

args.warrant: When one restaurant raises its menu prices 20 percent and the place next door doesn't, diners see the first as more expensive, even if the total bill is the same.
args.evidence: Lynn's research on restaurants that ended tipping, including falling online service ratings; restaurants that tried and dropped no-tipping policies.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the problem fades if all restaurants change together, which is what the resolution asks.

args.warrant: Tipping lets a customer reward a server who went out of the way and hold back for poor service. A fixed price takes that choice away.
args.evidence: Consumer surveys on tipping, such as those summarized by Lynn and Withiam, including a 1998 reader survey in which most preferred to choose their own tip over an automatic charge.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same research found a majority favored guaranteed server wages, and that a choice that barely tracks service isn't much of a reward.

args.claim: Tips keep labor costs flexible for small restaurants.
args.warrant: Restaurants run on thin margins. When pay rises and falls with sales, a slow month doesn't sink the business, which protects jobs.
args.evidence: Industry data on restaurant profit margins; reports from restaurant owners about the cost of moving to higher wages.
args.response: The affirmative replies that this shifts business risk onto workers, who then carry the slow months instead of the owner.

strawmen.strawman: They want to take money away from servers.
strawmen.why: Supporters want pay to be steadier and shared more fairly, and many expect wages to make up for lost tips.
strawmen.steelman: Tips barely track service, swing from shift to shift and leave kitchen workers out; building service into prices gives the whole staff steady pay and shows diners the real price.

strawmen.strawman: They just want restaurants to pay workers less.
strawmen.why: Defenders of tipping often argue that tips let skilled servers earn more than wages would.
strawmen.steelman: At many restaurants tips pay servers more than wages could, keep menu prices competitive and let diners reward good service.

weak.why: Tipping has been common in the United States for more than a century; argue about pay and prices, not labels.

weak.arg: If servers wanted more money, they'd get another job.
weak.why: It dodges the question of which pay system works better, and the same could be said of any job.

aff: How much would menu prices have to rise to replace tips?
What happens to a server who earns more from tips today than the new wage?
Why did some restaurants that tried this go back to tipping?
neg: How should a cook or dishwasher share in a good night?
If tips barely track service, what are they rewarding?
What happens to a server's rent payment after a slow week?
